recTjh2r9ceNB4puf.Bio: Tamara Sheville is the author of the Level Plane Poem series, six volumes of illustrated verse arguing that Earth is flat, level and motionless, covering curvature, surveying, navigation and celestial observation. Her sixth book, Flat Earth Fun-Damentals, makes the case that Earth is charted, mapped, flown, navigated, surveyed, engineered, constructed and measured flat. She has also written Nuclear Weapons Truth Bomb: An Explosion of Lies, a book length work in rhyming verse that takes apart the physics of the atomic bomb, a topic she approaches as a former member of the first civilian chemical biological terrorism response team.
recTjh2r9ceNB4puf.Name: Tamara Sheville

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title":"Rhymes Written For Her Parents","body":"Tamara traces her turn to a Dave Weiss interview she heard during the jab season, after which her brain ran nonstop and she filled thick notebooks. When Weiss ran a contest for short, concise flat earth proofs, she remembered the birthday card rhymes her grandfather used to write, and the Level Plane Poem series followed. She wanted something gentle enough for her veterinarian father and her OBGYN grandfather. Chance notes that the biggest problem with flat earth proponents is how easily they berate people who never had reason to question the globe, and Tamara calls the transition painful and gut wrenching."},{"title":"The Curvature Case In Court","body":"Much of the episode turns on a lawsuit. Tamara recounts Zen Garcia's fifteen thousand dollar challenge to demonstrate curvature with three repeatable, testable proofs. William Thompson believed he had done it, sued for the money, and lost, because he could not establish curvature beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. She pairs that with Nathan Oakley's book Measured Flat, arguing that every practical measurement, plumb, level, elevation, latitude, longitude and the compass, is taken from a horizontal plane of reference. Chance plays along on air, pointing north, south, east and west, and she calls that a flat plane of reference."},{"title":"Water, Containers, And Ice Walls","body":"Tamara carries a keychain bubble level and says the horizon stays at eye level from beaches, planes and balloons rather than dropping away on both sides. Water, she argues, is always flat and level, takes the shape of whatever holds it, and cannot keep its position without containment, which is why she treats Antarctica's tall shoreline cliffs as the rim of an enclosure rather than an edge to fall off. Chance stresses nobody claims a pizza floating in space, and raises the firmament dome, quoting Marty Leeds that everything beyond it is metaphysical. Tamara likens open gas beside a vacuum to propane without a tank."},{"title":"Polaris, Tides, And Terminator Lines","body":"The pair run through solar system mechanics. Tamara says a lit ball should show a clean terminator line and equal day and night, that tides rise on both sides of the planet while fresh water ignores the moon, and that gravity cannot hold the moon at 238,000 miles while astronauts float 250 miles up. Her Polaris poem multiplies six trillion miles by 433 light years to mock the scale, and she invokes the inverse square law. She points to the Georgia Guidestones hole always framing Polaris, and to Mercury and Venus appearing at dusk and dawn, dismissing refraction as the answer given for everything."},{"title":"Steelmanning The Globe On Air","body":"Chance says he spent days trying to falsify his own position, treating pole to pole circumnavigation as the strongest test, and found stories and a few photographs but no receipts. He plays a TikTok using a sculpture, a fiber optic camera and a toy boat, calling it a flawed experiment because a tabletop cannot reach the vanishing point, while granting that ships really do appear to vanish from the bottom up. Tamara answers with zooming in, perspective, and magnets in the Foucault pendulum. Chance concedes not every item in her books may hold up, yet says rocket thrust in a vacuum is heavy enough alone."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Can you actually prove the Earth is a rotating globe? Before recording this episode, I tried to falsify Flat Earth and find the strongest case for the conventional globe model, and couldn't. Tamara Sheville joins InnerVerse to put the globe on trial through a rapid-fire examination of curvature, level water, horizons, Antarctica, long-distance visibility, Polaris, atmospheric pressure, vacuum experiments, Foucault's pendulum, Earth rotation, gravity, planetary observations, and the classic disappearing-ship argument. This isn't built around one supposed “proof.” The question is: what happens when the assumptions behind the globe are examined one after another against measurement, observation and experiment.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Eight miles into the skin of an apple", "body": "Everything taught about the inside of the Earth rests on a hole that stopped short of eight miles down, which Tamara likens to not getting a third of the way through the skin of an apple. The Kola borehole crew guessed wrong about granite, water and gas every single time, heard sounds they could not explain, and quit when their machines failed. Chance pushes further and doubts the official account itself, because Soviet Russia reported 180 degrees Celsius at the bottom alongside liquid water, while the Mariana Trench a mile shallower stays freezing cold."}, {"title": "Eratosthenes on trial", "body": "The scholar wheeled out to prove the ancients already knew the Earth was a ball turns out to be thinly sourced. Tamara points out he barely appears in history books before the 1950s, Chance finds his work undiscovered until 1906 and traceable only through Renaissance era texts. The experiment itself needs a man to pace exactly five hundred miles in a straight line over rivers and houses, two cities to coordinate high noon simultaneously without clocks, and the sun to cast perfectly parallel rays, which is the very thing in question."}, {"title": "What the sun and the moon actually do", "body": "Chance argues we have lost the plot on the metaphysical properties of the two lights. Moonlight measures colder than shadow, things go damp at night under it and dry under the sun, and sunlight will lift a stain out of a shirt the way clotheslines quietly did for generations before dryers. Light on water lays down a long shimmering road to your feet rather than the single bright point a curved surface would give. Add the coincidence of a sun four hundred times bigger and four hundred times farther, and Tamara reads design rather than accident."}, {"title": "Straight lines where the curve should be", "body": "The engineering section is the most stubborn part of the case. Three hundred miles of Trans Australian railroad run dead flat across Western Australia where eleven miles of curvature should have been built in. The Suez Canal should carry a bulge of roughly 1,700 feet in its middle. The Nile drops about a foot over its entire length, measured from mean sea level, which is itself a horizontal plane of reference. Nobody surveys pipelines, highways or track with curvature in mind, and Tamara keeps returning to the simplest version: water never curves."}, {"title": "The models that cannot be made to work", "body": "Newton could not solve three bodies pulling on each other, and his answer was that God must periodically reach in and reset the clockwork, which Chance notes is a fine answer for a theist and a fatal one for materialist science. Tamara asks what would have happened if the apple had landed in water, where something heavier than air simply floats and gravity apparently stops applying. Then comes the plainest objection of all, that thrust requires something to push against, and Chance closes by saying not every item in a presentation has to land for the heavy hitters to stand."}]
